lines.text: Yale University. In a rare book library, a small book sits under strict guard, and nobody can read it. Its pages hold strange plants, women in green baths, and a script that exists nowhere else. Is it a message from another world?

Online, its writing is often called an alien alphabet. Others say a lost language, an unbreakable code, or the greatest hoax in history. For more than a century, the best codebreakers have failed to settle it.
So today we examine the book itself, one request at a time, the way a researcher would. This is the Voynich manuscript.
The Voynich manuscript. Evidence against theory. Fill in the first request slip.
Request one. Who held this book? Every real object has a paper trail, and this one has a longer trail than most people expect.
The trail begins in Prague in the sixteen-thirties. An alchemist named Georg Baresch owned a book he could not read, and it bothered him so much that he wrote to a famous scholar in Rome for help.
That scholar was Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit with a vast library and a reputation for solving puzzles. He is not known to have cracked this one.

In the mid sixteen-sixties, Baresch's friend Johannes Marcus Marci sent the book on to Kircher, with a letter that still survives. The letter repeats a story: Emperor Rudolf the Second once paid six hundred gold ducats for it.
The emperor, the letter says, believed the author was Roger Bacon, the thirteenth century English friar. Today, Yale calls the Bacon link pure speculation.
The dates break it. Bacon died around twelve ninety-two, and you will see in a moment that the parchment of this book is much younger than that.
Then the book vanishes into a Jesuit collection near Rome, and stays there for more than two centuries, until a rare book dealer comes looking.
In nineteen-twelve, a Polish-American dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought it. His name has been on it ever since.
After his death it passed to his wife Ethel, then to her friend Anne Nill, who sold it to a New York dealer in nineteen sixty-one.
In nineteen sixty-nine the dealer gave it to Yale's Beinecke Library, where it is catalogued as Manuscript four-oh-eight.
Since then it has left the building only once, for an exhibition on codes and ciphers at the Folger Shakespeare Library in twenty-fourteen.
So the first answer is plain. This is not a relic dropped from the sky, and not a mystery object with no history. It is a physical book with owners named in letters from the sixteen-thirties.
A book that Europeans were already puzzling over in the days of horse-drawn carts, centuries before anyone said the words flying saucer.
Request two. What is it made of, and when? Here, science can overrule any story.
The pages are parchment. Protein testing in twenty-fourteen showed it is calfskin.
In two thousand nine, the University of Arizona cut tiny samples from four pages and measured their carbon fourteen.
Carbon fourteen decays at a known rate once an animal dies. Measure what is left, correct it against tree rings, and you get a date for the skin.
All four samples agreed. With ninety-five percent probability, the animals died between fourteen-oh-four and fourteen thirty-eight.
That is the early fifteenth century, the decades of Joan of Arc, when printing had not yet reached Europe.
One caution. Carbon dating tells us when the animal died. It does not tell us when someone wrote on the skin.
Yale also reports chemical analysis of the inks and pigments, and says they fit materials used in fifteenth century manuscripts.
That sinks two stories. A forgery by Wilfrid Voynich would have needed old blank parchment and matching ink. And Roger Bacon died more than a century before these animals were born.
Yale's own cataloguers stay cautious. They place the book in central Europe, late fifteenth or sixteenth century, and scholars still debate how long after the parchment the writing came.
On dates, then, the case is strong. A real European book, from roughly the fifteenth century. Not ancient, and not otherworldly.
Now, the hands that made it.
Request three. Who wrote it? For years people pictured one lonely genius. The handwriting says otherwise.
In twenty-twenty, the medievalist Lisa Fagin Davis studied individual letter shapes: the angle of strokes, how a pen was lifted, how loops were closed. She found five different hands.
Two of those hands had been spotted decades earlier by the codebreaker Prescott Currier, who labelled them scribe one and scribe two. Davis added three more.
Five scribes suggests a workshop or a community. It does not look like one eccentric hoaxer scribbling alone. A critical paper has questioned the count of five, so the exact number is debated.
Davis also notes that the parchment is soft, the way a book becomes when it has been handled again and again. Someone used this book like a working manual.
Now a twist, published in October, twenty-twenty-six. Davis and Colin Layfield argue the book began as loose single folded sheets, each written by one scribe.
Then, they say, someone bound the sheets in the wrong order, perhaps without being able to read a word.
The clues: pictures that run off one page and reappear on another far away, and a water stain that does not match from page to page.
Layfield's computer analysis of about thirty-five thousand words found that some pages share vocabulary and others do not, which fits that idea.
If they are right, any study that assumed the current page order must be rethought. Davis is careful: we do not know if it is a code.
No alien hand here. Just scribes, quills, and a bookbinder who lost the thread.
Request four. What do the pictures show? Because we cannot read the words, the drawings are our only window.
First the herbal section, about a hundred and twenty-six pages, each with one or two plants. It looks like a normal medieval herbal, except almost none of the plants can be identified with certainty.
That has led some to say they grow on another world. There is no evidence for that. Medieval herbals were copied by hand, and drawings drifted a little with every copy.

The astronomical section has circular diagrams with suns, moons and stars, and twelve zodiac signs, including two fish for Pisces and a bull for Taurus. Those are the same signs Europeans used at the time.
In the zodiac rings, thirty women hold labelled stars. Strange, yes. But the layout is calendar-like, and the zodiac itself is plainly European.
Some see a galaxy in one circular drawing with curved arms. In nineteen-twenty-one, William Newbold read exactly that, a spiral galaxy that he said could only be seen through a telescope.
In nineteen thirty-one, John Manly showed the flaw. Newbold's method let letters be rearranged at will until Latin appeared, so it could prove almost anything.

The bathing section shows women in green pools linked by pipes and tubes. People have read it as plumbing, medicine, or something else. One twenty-twenty-four paper argued parts concern sex and conception. That is an interpretation, not a reading.
Then jars and roots that look like a pharmacy, and finally pages of text with small stars in the margins, perhaps recipes.
Put together, the pictures describe medicine, stars and bathing: ordinary medieval subjects, drawn in an unusual way. No spacecraft. No machines. No visitors.
Request five. The words themselves. About thirty-eight thousand of them, built from roughly two dozen symbols, written left to right.

Here is the strangest part. The text behaves like language. The most common word appears about twice as often as the second, and three times as often as the third, a pattern called Zipf's law, found in real languages.
In twenty-thirteen, the physicist Marcelo Montemurro found that words cluster by topic, the way keywords do in real books.

But it is also odd. Some words repeat up to five times in a row, and words that differ by one letter appear far too often. The famous codebreaker Elizebeth Friedman called the statistical hunt doomed to utter frustration.
Since nineteen twenty-one, claim after claim has appeared. Hebrew anagrams, abbreviated Latin, a lost Near Eastern language, Aztec Nahuatl. None has been independently verified.

In twenty-nineteen, a researcher announced he had read it in two weeks: a calligraphic proto-Romance language, written by nuns for a queen of Aragon. Within hours, Lisa Fagin Davis answered that proto-Romance is not a recognised language category.
She called such methods circular and aspirational: start with a guess from a picture, then search dictionaries until some word fits.
The other camp says there is no message. In two thousand three, Gordon Rugg showed that Voynich-like text can be generated from a table of prefixes, stems and suffixes, read through a paper grille.

But five scribes, calfskin parchment and a word pattern with topic clusters make a pure hoax an expensive and odd project. One team of linguists notes a much smaller hoax would have served the same purpose.
Time to score the case. Evidence on one side, theory on the other.

Parchment from fourteen-oh-four to fourteen thirty-eight: evidence. Owners named in letters from the sixteen-thirties: evidence. About five scribes in one workshop: likely. Language, cipher or hoax: unsolved.
Any claimed decipherment: not verified. Plants and stars from another world: no evidence. Alien authors: no evidence.
The verdict. Not aliens. The Voynich manuscript is a real European book, made of calfskin in the early fifteenth century, by about five scribes. What it says is still unknown.
That is the honest answer. The mystery is not that nobody on Earth could have written it. It is that somebody did, and we have not found the key.
And there are new keys. Put the pages back in their original order, and researchers can test whether the text starts to make sense. Davis says it moves the ball.
What lingers is a picture of a scribe, six hundred years ago, dipping a quill and writing something that mattered, for readers we cannot imagine.
Next case: tiny gold pendants from Colombia that look like airplanes. Ancient aircraft, or stylised animals?
What do you think the Voynich scribes were writing? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
